item.title: Game Petri Nets: Compositional Modeling and Analysis of Large-Scale Strategic Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.12779v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large-scale strategic systems, such as maintenance workflows, cyber campaigns, and multi-agent AI pipelines, consist of many interactions whose outcomes determine which later interactions become possible, who takes part, and with what resources. We introduce game Petri nets, formalized as outcome-driven compositional game Petri nets (OCGPNs), to model and analyze such systems. Local games are attached to places of a colored Petri net, and a game-to-token interface converts each resolved game into typed tokens that enable, synchronize, or block subsequent games. For general, concurrent nets, we give an operational semantics and a structural theory based on invariants and Farkas certificates, which shows that guards can certify unreachability whereas incentive instruments can only change values. For sequential nets, the net induces a stochastic game on its game places. We prove that global equilibria are exactly collections of equilibria of local games augmented by continuation values, characterize through successor-level pivotality when downstream games change upstream behavior, and compute values place by place via a decomposition into strongly connected components, at a cost additive in local game sizes. A composition calculus based on place fusion glues certificates across subnets and summarizes downstream subnets by their entry values. Two running examples, a maintenance workflow and an intrusion campaign derived from multi-resolution cyber-defense games, illustrate the theory, including the composition of a newly discovered attack scenario with an existing campaign.
item.dc:creator: Quanyan Zhu

item.title: The False Allure of "Security by Obscurity": A Game-Theoretic Approach
item.description: arXiv:2610.12858v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: "Security by obscurity," or the idea that hiding how a system works helps protect it from adversaries, has long been poorly regarded in the security community. Yet its intuitive appeal persists, and it has resurfaced repeatedly in industry practices and public debates over the years. The logic, on the one hand, is that open scrutiny of systems is the best way to find and respond to problems; and on the other hand, that too much openness can increase risk by giving adversaries a roadmap for attack. This isn't purely a technical question, but a human one: it's about how attackers and good-faith security researchers respond to openness in the real world. As such, security experts base their stance on decades of community experience; however, the field lacks empirical or theoretical foundations to back up these long-standing beliefs. We provide the first rigorous modeling of "security by obscurity," aiming to capture how rational actors will respond to openness or obscurity in fallible systems. We prove that in equilibrium under realistic model conditions, "obscured" systems are more likely to suffer successful attacks than "open" systems --- establishing theoretical support for the longstanding received wisdom.
item.dc:creator: In-Uck Park, Sunoo Park

item.title: Network Topology Shapes AI Intervention Effectiveness on Deception: Truth-Telling vs. Investigative Agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.12931v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deploying AI agents to combat dishonest communication is an intuitive response to deception in hybrid human-AI societies. However, the efficacy of such interventions in realistic networked settings remains unclear. We study this problem using an evolutionary game-theoretic model of the Deceiver's Game by extending it to structured networks, where agents can adopt deception, truth-telling, and investigation strategies. We introduce committed AI agents (zealots) fixed to either truth-telling or investigative strategies and conduct agent-based simulations across three network topologies. Our key findings are: (1) passive committed truth-telling agents can amplify adaptive deception by creating exploitable honest partners, whereas investigative agents increase adaptive truth-telling in the oscillatory regime; (2) intervention effects are non-monotonic in deployment density because committed agents reshape rather than simply suppress the underlying oscillatory dynamics; and (3) response peaks depend on topology, with sampled scale-free populations showing sharp low-density responses and fully connected populations requiring larger committed fractions. Overall, the results highlight the need to distinguish passive truth-telling from active investigation when using committed agents to influence networked deception dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Zhao Song, Stefan Sarkadi, The Anh Han

item.title: Limit-sure Winning in Team Games without Shared Randomness
item.description: arXiv:2610.13569v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study concurrent stochastic games in which a team of agents plays against an adversarial environment. If the agents could access a shared source of randomness, then these games reduce to two-player games. Despite being common in the literature on coalition games, this assumption does not accurately model real-world systems. In this paper, we consider the setting where the agents only have access to individual sources of randomness, and must satisfy a given reachability or safety objective. The limit-sure problem asks whether the team can ensure that the objective is satisfied with probability at least $1-\lambda$ for every $\lambda>0$. For reachability objectives, we show that this problem is $\mathsf{NP}$-complete. For safety objectives, we show that limit-sure winning coincides with almost-sure winning, which is known to lie in $\mathsf{P}$. As a corollary of these results, we conclude that model checking of the qualitative fragment of the logic Individually Randomised ATL -- introduced in the recent work of Brice et al. -- is $\mathsf{P}^{\mathsf{NP}}$-complete.
item.dc:creator: L\'eonard Brice, Thomas A. Henzinger, Alipasha Montaseri, Ali Shafiee, K. S. Thejaswini

item.title: Complexity of Autobidding Equilibria in GSP Sponsored Shopping
item.description: arXiv:2610.13716v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We revisit autobidding equilibria in GSP sponsored shopping auctions, recently proposed and studied in D\"utting et al. On the existence side, we show that autobidding equilibria under both budget constraints (ABE-B) and return-on-investment constraints (ABE-R) always exist and, moreover, always admit equilibria with polynomial-size support over the allocation space. On the computational side, we show that computing an exact equilibrium is in FIXP, and that computing an approximate equilibrium is in PPAD. We also prove that computing an approximate equilibrium is PPAD-hard for both ABE-B and ABE-R. Together, these results provide a fairly comprehensive picture of the computational complexity of autobidding equilibria in GSP sponsored shopping auctions.
item.dc:creator: Kristoffer Arnsfelt Hansen, Yuhao Li, Xinhao Nie

item.title: The Distortion of Threshold Approval Multiwinner Voting
item.description: arXiv:2610.13725v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study multiwinner voting with $n$ voters and $m$ candidates, where the goal is to select a committee of size $k$. Voters have unit-sum cardinal utilities but report only coarse information induced by $t$ utility thresholds. In particular, each voter partitions the candidates into approval sets, with the utilities of all candidates in the same set lying between the same pair of consecutive thresholds. We model the utility of each voter for a committee as a normalized monotone symmetric norm, capturing, among others, additive welfare, best-representative utility, top-$r$ welfare, $\ell_p$ welfare, and normalized non-increasing ordered weighted averages. We design a deterministic rule with distortion at most $2(2m)^{1/t}$ and a randomized rule with distortion at most $2\min\{m^{1/(t+1)},m/k\}$. These guarantees hold for every committee size $k$ and every norm in our framework. Consequently, a single threshold yields distortion $O(m)$ for deterministic rules and $O(\sqrt{m})$ for randomized rules, while $O(\log m)$ thresholds suffice for constant distortion. We complement these results with norm-dependent lower bounds that asymptotically match our upper bounds for constant committee sizes, including the single-winner case.
item.dc:creator: Mohamad Latifian, Marzieh Nilipour, Alexandros A. Voudouris

item.title: Asymmetric Information in Dynamic Lending Games
item.description: arXiv:2610.13759v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a dynamic lending game with limited but reusable supply. Borrower arrivals and loan durations are stochastic. Demand is allocated cheapest-first, subject to available supply, so a lender's quote affects both its current payoff and its ability to serve future borrowers. Motivated by industry practice, we study this problem through the lens of information disclosure: Lenders observe either only their own available supply or also their rivals' aggregate available supply. We ask how providing this information to all, some or none of the lenders affects payoffs as demand varies relative to supply, and how these effects change when a fixed total supply is divided among different numbers of lenders. Interestingly, in the case of asymmetric information disclosure, total payoffs can increase, while total lending remains the same. We identify sufficient mathematical regimes in which this phenomenon occurs. Who receives supply information matters differently as demand rises. For the case of two lenders, informing only the larger lender yields higher total lender payoff at lower demand, while informing only the smaller lender can yield the highest total lender payoff at higher demand. For a platform deciding which lenders can observe rival supply, the results suggest that disclosure can change the fees paid by borrowers without changing how much is lent. Wider access to supply information need not lower those fees: its effect depends on who receives the information and the balance between demand and supply.
item.dc:creator: Kristijan Atanasov, Frederik Mallmann-Trenn, Carmine Ventre

item.title: A $1/2$-Approximation for Pandora's Problem with Deadlines
item.description: arXiv:2610.13775v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pandora's problem is a fundamental model of sequential search in which opening each box incurs a cost. We study the variant with deadlines, where each box has a publicly known deadline for both opening and selection. We prove that a simple threshold strategy achieves a $1/2$-approximation to the optimal expected utility, improving the previous guarantee of $(e-1)/(4e)\approx0.158$ due to Berger et al. (AAAI 2024).
item.dc:creator: Shenyu Qin, Chihao Zhang, Yuhao Zhang, Zixuan Zhu

item.title: Dynamic Matching with Abandonment: Optimal Guarantees via Static Priority Policies
item.description: arXiv:2610.12991v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study stochastic dynamic matching with abandonment, a fundamental model in which agents of different types arrive over time, may abandon the market while waiting, and can be matched in pairs for rewards that depend on their types. No online policy can guarantee more than $0.5$ of the omniscient benchmark, which knows all arrival and departure times. Whether this guarantee is achievable has been a central open problem, even in special cases. We resolve this problem by showing that, on every instance, a simple static priority policy, which is computable in polynomial time, earns at least $0.5$ of the omniscient benchmark. This establishes that the optimal competitive ratio is exactly $0.5$, improving the previous best guarantee of 0.192 for the general model [Li et al. 2026; Collina et al. 2020] Our analysis rests on a key stochastic result, which is a new lower bound on the probability that some agent from a given set of types is available. Building on this bound, we develop two approaches: a primal approach that reads the priorities from an optimal solution of a novel linear program, and a dual approach that assigns a ``value'' to each type, and prioritizes matches with high ``surplus'' (reward minus value of involved agents). These values are the unique solution of a fixed-point equation derived from linear programming duality. We also show that the two approaches are closely connected.
item.dc:creator: Nick Arnosti, Rad Niazadeh, Pranav Nuti, Felipe Simon

item.title: Co-opetition Equilibrium in Adversarial Team Games with Heterogeneous Utilities
item.description: arXiv:2512.18989v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The United Nations' 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development requires all countries to collaborate against adversarial factors, a scenario that can be formalized as an adversarial team game. However, existing solution concepts assume team players share identical utility functions---an assumption inconsistent with real-world settings where countries have divergent objectives. This paper argues that studying adversarial team games must account for heterogeneous utilities among team players. We show that ignoring utility differences can render computed equilibria unstable in the original game, and we formalize this degradation via the Price of Ignoring Heterogeneity, which can be unbounded. To address this, we introduce the Co-opetition Equilibrium (CoE), where team players with heterogeneous utilities correlate their strategies (cooperation) against an adversary (competition). We establish existence via reduction from Nash equilibrium, and prove that finding a CoE is PPAD-complete while computing a Team-Maximizing CoE (TMCoE) is NP-hard. Nevertheless, we identify a broad class of zero-sum adversarial team games---those satisfying a consistent-constraint condition that generalizes identical utilities---where TMCoEs are exchangeable and computable in polynomial time via linear programming. We outline directions for algorithm design, MARL, and extensions to extensive-form and multi-team games.
item.dc:creator: Youzhi Zhang

item.title: Smart Lotteries in School Choice: Ex-ante Pareto-Improvement with Ex-post Stability
item.description: arXiv:2602.10679v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In school choice, students typically have strict preferences over the schools while the schools have coarse priorities over the students based on their distance and their enrolled siblings. The outcome of a centralized admission mechanism is then usually obtained by the Deferred Acceptance (DA) algorithm with random tie-breaking. Therefore, every outcome of this mechanism that occurs with a positive probability is a stable solution for the coarse priorities. This implies a probabilistic assignment, specifying the admission probability for each student-school pair. In this paper, we propose a new efficiency-improving stable 'smart lottery' mechanism. We aim to improve the probabilistic assignment ex-ante in a stochastic dominance sense, while ensuring that the improved random matching is still ex-post stable, meaning that it can be decomposed into stable matchings regarding the original coarse priorities. Therefore, this smart lottery mechanism can provide a clear Pareto-improvement in expectation for any cardinal utilities compared to the standard DA with lottery solution, without sacrificing the stability of the final outcome. We show that although the underlying computational problem is NP-hard, we can solve the problem in practice by using column generation. Our computational results show that the welfare gains by our mechanism are substantially larger than the expected gains by standard methods that realize efficiency improvements after ties have already been broken. Additionally, we illustrate for real-world school choice data of Ghent (Belgium) that, while not theoretically guaranteed, our mechanism can Pareto-improve upon methods that improve upon DA but violate ex-post stability, such as Efficiency-Adjusted Deferred Acceptance.
item.dc:creator: Haris Aziz, P\'eter Bir\'o, Gergely Cs\'aji, Tom Demeulemeester

item.title: Indirect Geoeconomic Influence: A Switching Dynamical Systems Framework for Mechanism Design
item.description: arXiv:2608.07940v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop a formal framework for analyzing indirect geoeconomic influence. The influencing state (sender) does not attempt to change a target nation's policy directly. Instead, the sender restructures the target's internal political economy so that its own citizens, firms, and institutions generate the compliance pressure. The framework rests on a switching dynamical system (SDS) in which a target's political economy evolves under mode-dependent rules. We analyze two modes: a permissive mode, in which a mechanism transmits pressure toward the sender's preferred policy, and a contested mode, entered naturally once the target detects and attributes the mechanism. Crucially, the sender's mechanism design shapes the transition into the contested mode. Our approach inverts the usual regime-switching problem in which analysts estimate a latent transition kernel from data. The indirect influence approach is to have the designer engineer a kernel to steep regime occupancy over a planning horizon. A structured switch vector decomposes any mechanism along discrete design dimensions, and a combinatorial optimizer searches this space for high-performing archetypes scored on compliance, time-to-threshold, and a durability ratio. We characterize mode-conditional equilibria and derive comparative statics on credibility and legibility, showing that the legibility penalty is scaled by the salience of the government channel and interacts with the mechanism's cost incidence. We illustrate the framework with two stylized mechanisms and report a two-part proof of concept: a simulation of 972 archetypes, and a fully crossed study of the pipeline's optional generative stage in which language models write and blindly classify candidate instruments for archetypes.
item.dc:creator: Nikolos Gurney, Boxi Fu, Soham Hans, Volkan Ustun

item.title: Protocol effects on feature-based hardware-Trojan detection across Trust-Hub families
item.description: arXiv:2609.07199v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Trust-Hub reuses host circuits: several files differ mainly in the inserted Trojan. When gates from sibling variants enter both training and test folds, a detector can benefit from host logic it has already seen. We measure that effect instead of proposing another classifier. The corpus contains 49,124 gates from 16 netlists grouped into five host families. We left the parser, 36 gate features, class weighting, model settings, threshold, and family-level aggregation unchanged and altered one choice: the test boundary. The three settings draw test gates from the pooled corpus, withhold a complete netlist, or withhold every variant of one host. The choice matters. Random forest records F1/AP of 0.914/0.978 with pooled gates, 0.636/0.851 with one netlist held out, and 0.460/0.577 with a host family held out. XGBoost falls from 0.946/0.976 to 0.464/0.544 across the same comparison. Logistic regression loses AP, although its fixed-threshold F1 is not monotonic. Each family shows the same pooled-to-family direction. Feature removal, repeated model and simulator seeds, score normalization, parser-related exclusions, and a smaller sample change the size of the gap without reversing it. Aggregation also matters: a gate-weighted average is dominated by the larger ISCAS files, so the headline values give each host family one vote. Bootstrap and jackknife summaries keep the gap positive, but their folds reuse training families. We treat the five family rows as descriptive evidence rather than independent trials. Five host families are too few for a population claim, and the experiment says nothing about transfer to a new cell library or an industrial design. It supports a narrower conclusion: sibling benchmark variants can inflate apparent transfer. Benchmarks with several variants of one host circuit should report family-aware holdouts and all five family results beside pooled scores.
item.dc:creator: Hang Xiao, Chuhong Xu, Kainan Zhou, Gangzhen Qian, Lu Yi

item.title: Explicit Asymptotic Bounds for Sequential Calibration Beyond $T^{2/3}$
item.description: arXiv:2610.07623v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Probability forecasts are calibrated when predicted probabilities match empirical outcome frequencies: among events assigned a probability $p$, we'd hope that the fraction of positive outcomes is close to $p$. We study the problem of sequential forecasting of binary outcomes. The classical $O(T^{2/3})$ bound on expected cumulative $\ell_1$-calibration error established by Foster and Vohra stood for over two decades until Dagan et al. reduced the exponent $2/3$ by an unspecified constant. We establish a new two-phase recursive labeling strategy for the sign-preservation-with-reuse game that yields the bound $O(n^{\alpha}t^\beta)$ for all choices of space and time. We then sharpen the reduction from upper bounds on sign preservation to calibration by modifying the equivalence of Dagan et al. to use only $O(\log T)$ instances of the sign-preservation-with-reuse game. This lets us establish an explicit bound of $O(T^{0.662942288})$, the first explicit exponent below $2/3$ for sequential calibration, by combining both improvements and choosing explicit feasible parameters.
item.dc:creator: Eric Dai, Maxwell Fishelson

item.title: Efficient Algorithms for Online Subadditive Combinatorial Allocations
item.description: arXiv:2610.09050v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: For the online combinatorial allocation problem with subadditive valuations, Correa and Cristi (STOC 2023) proved the existence of a $6$-competitive online algorithm, improving on the previous best $O(\log\!\log m)$-competitive online algorithm due to D\"utting, Kesselheim, and Lucier (FOCS 2020), where $m$ is the number of items. However, Correa and Cristi's result is existential, and it was left open whether a constant competitive ratio is attainable via an efficient online algorithm that uses a polynomial number of demand oracle queries. In this work, we answer this affirmatively, giving an expected-polynomial-time $(6 + \epsilon)$-competitive online algorithm for any constant $\epsilon > 0$. Our techniques also recover, in the offline setting, the $(2 + \epsilon)$-approximation result of Feige (STOC, 2006). Finally, when the buyers' valuations are drawn from identical distributions, we exploit symmetry to obtain an improved $(60/11+\epsilon)$-competitive algorithm. Starting with the natural configuration LP relaxation for the problem, our main technical contribution is a recursive Bundle Score Generator (BSG) that resolves item conflicts by assigning correlated scores to the items requested by each buyer. Unlike the Random Score Generator whose existence is shown by Correa and Cristi, our BSG is efficiently computable in expected polynomial time. Moreover, it satisfies a stochastic dominance property that is sufficient to recover both Feige's offline result and Correa and Cristi's online result.
item.dc:creator: Calum MacRury, Rian Neogi, Kanstantsin Pashkovich, Sahil Singla, Siddharth M Sundaram, Chaitanya Swamy
